newsitem.title: USA: New MIT policy protects ROTC gays financially.
newsitem.headline: New MIT policy protects ROTC gays financially.

text.p: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology will guarantee financial aid packages to its ROTC students whose military funding is cut because of their sexual orientation, the school said Friday.

"For years now we have been struggling with this military regulation against homosexuality," Sarah Gallop, an assistant to MIT President Charles Vest, said. "There are two principles at MIT that we hold dear. One is our longstanding and deep commitment to national service ... an equally important principle for us is to promote an environment of nondiscrimination."

Under the policy, which was not formally announced but went into effect Wednesday, any MIT Reserve Officer Training Corps student whose federal scholarship is terminated because of sexual orientation is encouraged to apply for financial aid to continue their education.

MIT will forgive supplemental loans to students who perform full-time public service after leaving the school, including VISTA or the Peace Corps service or teaching in grades kindergarten through high school.
MIT shares its ROTC programme, which had 221 students enrolled during the Fall 1995-96 term -- the last official figures available, with Harvard and Tufts Universities as well as Wellesley College.

None of the students enrolled in ROTC has had a scholarship terminated since the Department of Defence's "don't ask, don't tell, don't pursue" policy regarding sexual orientation was enacted in 1993, MIT said.

Harvard spokesman Joe Wrinn said, "We provide full-needs aid to all students and should a change like this affect a student's need we would, of course, take this into consideration and welcome them to re-apply for the additional aid."
A spokeswoman for Tufts University said that a faculty task force submitted recommendations to the university's president last week, but those recommendations had not yet become public.

"All Wellesley students are eligible to apply for financial aid, which is given on the basis of financial need," Wellesley spokeswoman Janet Mendelsohn said. "So, if any students loses a scholarship from any other source they are welcome to apply for financial aid."
